after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,\text{_____}⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $r(u,v)$ parametrizes the surface defined in Cartesian coordinates as 
${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{3}=0.$
 What is the third component of $r?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation of the surface in the form $z=f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{3} & =0 \\ z & =\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, a point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
r=⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩=⟨x,\,y,\,\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}⟩.
$$

 

Finally, setting $x=u$ and $y=v,$ we obtain the vector function that parametrizes the surface:

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,\sqrt[3]{{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}}⟩
$$

Therefore, the third component of $r$ is $\sqrt[3]{{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}}.$

decision.explanation: Multiplying the surface equation by 6 gives x+y+3(z-1)=1, so 3z=4-x-y. Substituting x=u and y=v yields z=(4-u-v)/3.

after.problem:
$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,\text{_____}⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $r(u,v)$ parametrizes the surface defined in Cartesian coordinates as 
$\frac{x+y}{6}+\frac{z-1}{2}=\frac{1}{6}.$
 What is the third component of $r?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation of the surface in the form $z=f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+y}{6}+\frac{z-1}{2} & =\frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{z-1}{2} & =\frac{1}{6}-\frac{x+y}{6} \\ \frac{z-1}{2} & =\frac{1-x-y}{6} \\ z & =\frac{4-x-y}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, a point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
r=⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩=⟨x,\,y,\,\frac{4-x-y}{3}⟩.
$$

 

Finally, setting $x=u$ and $y=v,$ we obtain the vector function that parametrizes the surface:

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,\frac{4-u-v}{3}⟩
$$

Therefore, the third component of $r$ is $\frac{4-u-v}{3}.$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
$$
f(r,\theta )=⟨r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{_____}⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $f(r,\theta )$ parametrizes the surface defined in cylindrical polar coordinates as 
$4{r}^{2}-{z}^{2}=0$
for $z\ge 0.$ What is the third component of $f?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation of the surface in the form $z=f(r,\theta ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{r}^{2}-{z}^{2} & =0 \\ {z}^{2} & =4{r}^{2} \\ z & =\sqrt{4{r}^{2}} \\ z & =2r\end{aligned}
$$

We disregard the negative solution since we are given that $z\ge 0.$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and $(x,y,z)$ are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

Now, a point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
f=⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩=⟨r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩.
$$

Finally, substituting $z=2r,$ we obtain

$$
f(r,\theta )=⟨r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,2r⟩.
$$

Therefore, the third component of $f$ is $2r.$

content.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation of the surface in the form $\rho =f(\theta ,ϕ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}ϕ & =\rho \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta  \\ \rho  & =ϕ\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Now, a point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

$$
f=⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩=⟨\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩.
$$

Finally, substituting $\rho =ϕ\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\theta ,ϕ) & =⟨ϕ\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,ϕ\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,ϕ\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩ \\  & =⟨ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,ϕ\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,ϕ\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the first component of $f$ is $ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$
